title: Hagia Sophia (537)
hookLine: a dome that seemed to hang from heaven; a later story says Justinian claimed he'd outdone Solomon

cards: A historian named Procopius walks into a new church in Constantinople and tries to describe the roof. He can't quite manage it. The great dome, he writes, doesn't seem to rest on stone at all.
It seems to hang from heaven on a golden chain. And the light doesn't seem to come in from outside; it seems to be born inside the place.

There's a later story, too, that the emperor Justinian walked in on the day it was dedicated and said he had outdone Solomon, who built the temple in Jerusalem. Whether he said it or not, the story stuck.

teach.h: HOLY WISDOM, NOT A SAINT'S NAME.
teach.b: Hagia Sophia is Greek for holy wisdom. The church wasn't named for a saint called Sophia. It was named for the wisdom of God, and Paul, in the King James words, calls Christ "the wisdom of God."
The book of Proverbs pictures wisdom as a builder: "Wisdom hath builded her house." Here was a house built in her name. Procopius, who wrote about the emperor's buildings, is our eyewitness.
He describes a dome so wide and so light it seemed to float, with a ring of windows around its base, so the sun pours in just below the curve.
That's the trick behind the hanging dome: the light comes in under it, and the solid part seems to lift off. Now the Solomon story.

The Bible's Solomon, dedicating his own temple, said something humbler: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?"
The builder of the temple in Jerusalem says no house can hold God. Some readers hear that as the honest center of any great church. The dome isn't a container for God.

teach.h: A SHAPE THAT POINTS PAST ITSELF.
teach.b: It's a shape that points past itself, stone and light trying to say something about heaven.
Hagia Sophia has had a long life since: a cathedral, then a mosque, then a museum, and today a mosque again, prayed in by Muslims and visited by people of every faith and none.
Orthodox Christians still remember it as the great church of Constantinople.

how: Orthodox Christians remember Hagia Sophia as the great church of Constantinople, and some Orthodox churches are built around a central dome with an image of Christ looking down from its center.

games.q: you're Solomon, dedicating the temple you built for God. what do you say about it?
o: at last, God has a house worthy of him.
will God indeed dwell on the earth? heaven can't contain him, much less this house.
games.why: Solomon's prayer admits that the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, "how much less this house that I have builded?"

practice: Find a photo of the inside of Hagia Sophia's dome, looking straight up, or picture one. Let your eyes go first to the ring of windows, then up into the curve, then to the very top, without analyzing.
If you pray, let Solomon's question sit with you as you look; if you don't, simply notice what happens in you when you look up for a long time.
